findings.body: Unhandled AttributeError (`'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`) produces a 500 for all non-member/token-authenticated callers, breaking a previously working endpoint.
findings.failure_mode: Endpoint raises AttributeError and returns 500 instead of the audit log listing.
findings.impact: Unhandled AttributeError (`'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`) produces a 500 for all non-member/token-authenticated callers, breaking a previously working endpoint.
findings.root_cause: The new eligibility check dereferences `organization_context.member` without handling the documented case that `member` is None when the requester has no membership.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard for None membership, e.g. `enable_advanced = is_active_superuser(request) or (organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access)`, or move the evaluation inside the `use_optimized` branch with a None check.
findings.title: AttributeError when organization member is None (e.g. API-key / non-member auth) crashes every audit log request
findings.trigger: Any GET to the audit logs endpoint where `organization_context.member` is None and `request.user.is_superuser` is falsy — e.g. authentication via an org API key or org auth token with `org:write` scope (request.user is AnonymousUser, member is None). This line executes unconditionally on every request, regardless of the `optimized_pagination` param.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 71 verbatim shows `organization_context.member.has_global_access` without None check. RpcUserOrganizationContext model (L346) documents `member: RpcOrganizationMember | None = None` - member is None when user has no membership. This executes unconditionally before the `use_optimized` branch, causing AttributeError for API-key/token auth where member is None.

raw_findings.body: The supposedly restricted negative-offset pagination path (comments claim it is for 'authorized administrators') is reachable by ordinary members and by superusers without an elevated session, defeating the stated authorization intent.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Authorization check silently grants the privileged pagination mode to unintended principals.
raw_findings.impact: The supposedly restricted negative-offset pagination path (comments claim it is for 'authorized administrators') is reachable by ordinary members and by superusers without an elevated session, defeating the stated authorization intent.
raw_findings.root_cause: Gate built on `has_global_access` (a project-visibility flag defaulting to True) and the raw `is_superuser` model flag, neither of which encodes 'administrator'.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: If the gate must exist, use `is_active_superuser(request)` and an actual admin/role check (e.g. role scopes) instead of `has_global_access`; better, remove the special path entirely.
raw_findings.title: "Admin-only" gate is ineffective: has_global_access defaults True for regular members and raw is_superuser bypasses active-superuser check
raw_findings.trigger: Any org member requests `?optimized_pagination=true`: `OrganizationMember.has_global_access` defaults to True (models/organizationmember.py:216), so nearly all members pass this gate; additionally `request.user.is_superuser` checks the dormant DB flag rather than `is_active_superuser(request)` as the sibling permission class does.

raw_findings.body: Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing; `queryset[-5:...]` raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` which is not a `BadPaginationError`, so the request returns a 500 instead of a 400. The accompanying comments ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level', 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') are factually wrong and, had the slice worked, the stated intent of 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' would itself be a data-exposure design flaw.

            stop = start_offset + limit + extra
            results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])
raw_findings.failure_mode: Crafted cursor causes an unhandled exception (500) on the audit logs endpoint; comments mislead future maintainers into believing the behavior is safe.

raw_findings.root_cause: New code deliberately forwards attacker-controlled negative cursor offsets into Django queryset slicing based on a false assumption about ORM behavior.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Remove the negative-offset branch entirely; reject cursors with `offset < 0` by raising `BadPaginationError` so they surface as a 400 ParseError.
raw_findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset path slices a QuerySet with a negative index, raising unhandled ValueError
raw_findings.trigger: A caller eligible for `enable_advanced_features` supplies a crafted cursor such as `cursor=0:-5:0` (Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets) with `optimized_pagination=true`.

raw_findings.body: `math.ceil(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, so every optimized-path request with results returns a 500; pagination cursors can never be built.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Runtime TypeError during cursor construction turns the optimized pagination path into a guaranteed 500.
raw_findings.impact: `math.ceil(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, so every optimized-path request with results returns a 500; pagination cursors can never be built.
raw_findings.root_cause: The new paginator copied the numeric `Paginator.get_item_key` implementation while being wired to a datetime `order_by` key at its only call site.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Convert datetime values like `DateTimePaginator.get_item_key` does (strftime to epoch * multiplier) or make `OptimizedCursorPaginator` derive from `DateTimePaginator` instead of copying `Paginator`'s numeric key logic.
raw_findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to datetime values, crashing on the datetime-ordered audit log queryset
raw_findings.trigger: Any eligible request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row: the endpoint instantiates this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, "datetime")` yields a `datetime` object, and `build_cursor` invokes `get_item_key` on the first/last result.

raw_findings.body: PostgreSQL cannot compare timestamp to integer, producing a database error (500), or at best incorrect filtering; contrast with `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor`, which converts the cursor value back to a tz-aware datetime.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Second-page requests on the optimized path fail with a database type error or return wrong rows.
raw_findings.impact: PostgreSQL cannot compare timestamp to integer, producing a database error (500), or at best incorrect filtering; contrast with `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor`, which converts the cursor value back to a tz-aware datetime.
raw_findings.root_cause: The paginator reuses `Paginator`'s identity `value_from_cursor` despite being bound to a datetime sort key.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Convert the cursor value back to a datetime (mirror `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor` with the same multiplier) or reuse `DateTimePaginator` semantics wholesale.
raw_findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns raw cursor integer that is compared against a datetime column
raw_findings.trigger: A follow-up page request on the optimized path with a non-zero cursor value: `build_queryset` injects the raw integer into the SQL predicate `"{col} <= %s"` against the `datetime` column.

raw_findings.body: Invalid cursors are no longer surfaced as errors on the forward path (clients silently get the first page, breaking pagination invariants), while the prev path still raises Django's `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` as a 500 — directly contradicting the new comment that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. This change affects every list endpoint sharing BasePaginator.

validated_findings.body: Unhandled AttributeError (`'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`) produces a 500 for all non-member/token-authenticated callers, breaking a previously working endpoint.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Endpoint raises AttributeError and returns 500 instead of the audit log listing.
validated_findings.impact: Unhandled AttributeError (`'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`) produces a 500 for all non-member/token-authenticated callers, breaking a previously working endpoint.
validated_findings.root_cause: The new eligibility check dereferences `organization_context.member` without handling the documented case that `member` is None when the requester has no membership.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Guard for None membership, e.g. `enable_advanced = is_active_superuser(request) or (organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access)`, or move the evaluation inside the `use_optimized` branch with a None check.
validated_findings.title: AttributeError when organization member is None (e.g. API-key / non-member auth) crashes every audit log request
validated_findings.trigger: Any GET to the audit logs endpoint where `organization_context.member` is None and `request.user.is_superuser` is falsy — e.g. authentication via an org API key or org auth token with `org:write` scope (request.user is AnonymousUser, member is None). This line executes unconditionally on every request, regardless of the `optimized_pagination` param.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Line 71 verbatim shows `organization_context.member.has_global_access` without None check. RpcUserOrganizationContext model (L346) documents `member: RpcOrganizationMember | None = None` - member is None when user has no membership. This executes unconditionally before the `use_optimized` branch, causing AttributeError for API-key/token auth where member is None.

validated_findings.body: The supposedly restricted negative-offset pagination path (comments claim it is for 'authorized administrators') is reachable by ordinary members and by superusers without an elevated session, defeating the stated authorization intent.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Authorization check silently grants the privileged pagination mode to unintended principals.
validated_findings.impact: The supposedly restricted negative-offset pagination path (comments claim it is for 'authorized administrators') is reachable by ordinary members and by superusers without an elevated session, defeating the stated authorization intent.
validated_findings.root_cause: Gate built on `has_global_access` (a project-visibility flag defaulting to True) and the raw `is_superuser` model flag, neither of which encodes 'administrator'.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: If the gate must exist, use `is_active_superuser(request)` and an actual admin/role check (e.g. role scopes) instead of `has_global_access`; better, remove the special path entirely.
validated_findings.title: "Admin-only" gate is ineffective: has_global_access defaults True for regular members and raw is_superuser bypasses active-superuser check
validated_findings.trigger: Any org member requests `?optimized_pagination=true`: `OrganizationMember.has_global_access` defaults to True (models/organizationmember.py:216), so nearly all members pass this gate; additionally `request.user.is_superuser` checks the dormant DB flag rather than `is_active_superuser(request)` as the sibling permission class does.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Line 71 uses `request.user.is_superuser` (DB flag) instead of `is_active_superuser(request)` as used in OrganizationAuditPermission (L124). Also `has_global_access` defaults True per model (L216). The gate intended for 'authorized administrators' is ineffective - regular members pass via has_global_access=True.

validated_findings.body: Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing; `queryset[-5:...]` raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` which is not a `BadPaginationError`, so the request returns a 500 instead of a 400. The accompanying comments ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level', 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') are factually wrong and, had the slice worked, the stated intent of 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' would itself be a data-exposure design flaw.
validated_findings.evidence:
start_offset = cursor.offset  # Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination
            stop = start_offset + limit + extra
            results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])
validated_findings.failure_mode: Crafted cursor causes an unhandled exception (500) on the audit logs endpoint; comments mislead future maintainers into believing the behavior is safe.
validated_findings.impact: Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing; `queryset[-5:...]` raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` which is not a `BadPaginationError`, so the request returns a 500 instead of a 400. The accompanying comments ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level', 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') are factually wrong and, had the slice worked, the stated intent of 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' would itself be a data-exposure design flaw.
validated_findings.root_cause: New code deliberately forwards attacker-controlled negative cursor offsets into Django queryset slicing based on a false assumption about ORM behavior.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Remove the negative-offset branch entirely; reject cursors with `offset < 0` by raising `BadPaginationError` so they surface as a 400 ParseError.
validated_findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset path slices a QuerySet with a negative index, raising unhandled ValueError
validated_findings.trigger: A caller eligible for `enable_advanced_features` supplies a crafted cursor such as `cursor=0:-5:0` (Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets) with `optimized_pagination=true`.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Lines 880-882 show `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where start_offset can be negative (cursor.offset < 0). Django QuerySets raise ValueError on negative slicing. Comment at L876 falsely claims 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'.

validated_findings.body: `math.ceil(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, so every optimized-path request with results returns a 500; pagination cursors can never be built.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Runtime TypeError during cursor construction turns the optimized pagination path into a guaranteed 500.
validated_findings.impact: `math.ceil(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, so every optimized-path request with results returns a 500; pagination cursors can never be built.
validated_findings.root_cause: The new paginator copied the numeric `Paginator.get_item_key` implementation while being wired to a datetime `order_by` key at its only call site.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Convert datetime values like `DateTimePaginator.get_item_key` does (strftime to epoch * multiplier) or make `OptimizedCursorPaginator` derive from `DateTimePaginator` instead of copying `Paginator`'s numeric key logic.
validated_findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to datetime values, crashing on the datetime-ordered audit log queryset
validated_findings.trigger: Any eligible request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row: the endpoint instantiates this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, "datetime")` yields a `datetime` object, and `build_cursor` invokes `get_item_key` on the first/last result.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Lines 838-840 show `get_item_key` calling `math.floor(value)` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. Endpoint uses `order_by="-datetime"` so key is 'datetime', value is datetime object. math.floor/ceil on datetime raises TypeError.

validated_findings.body: PostgreSQL cannot compare timestamp to integer, producing a database error (500), or at best incorrect filtering; contrast with `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor`, which converts the cursor value back to a tz-aware datetime.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Second-page requests on the optimized path fail with a database type error or return wrong rows.
validated_findings.impact: PostgreSQL cannot compare timestamp to integer, producing a database error (500), or at best incorrect filtering; contrast with `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor`, which converts the cursor value back to a tz-aware datetime.
validated_findings.root_cause: The paginator reuses `Paginator`'s identity `value_from_cursor` despite being bound to a datetime sort key.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Convert the cursor value back to a datetime (mirror `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor` with the same multiplier) or reuse `DateTimePaginator` semantics wholesale.
validated_findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns raw cursor integer that is compared against a datetime column
validated_findings.trigger: A follow-up page request on the optimized path with a non-zero cursor value: `build_queryset` injects the raw integer into the SQL predicate `"{col} <= %s"` against the `datetime` column.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Lines 842-843 show `value_from_cursor` returns raw `cursor.value` (integer). When used with datetime column in build_queryset, SQL compares timestamp to integer causing database type error. DateTimePaginator (L238-240) properly converts via fromtimestamp.

validated_findings.body: Invalid cursors are no longer surfaced as errors on the forward path (clients silently get the first page, breaking pagination invariants), while the prev path still raises Django's `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` as a 500 — directly contradicting the new comment that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. This change affects every list endpoint sharing BasePaginator.

validated_findings.failure_mode: Core pagination either silently accepts malformed cursors or crashes with an unhandled ValueError depending on cursor direction.
validated_findings.impact: Invalid cursors are no longer surfaced as errors on the forward path (clients silently get the first page, breaking pagination invariants), while the prev path still raises Django's `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` as a 500 — directly contradicting the new comment that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. This change affects every list endpoint sharing BasePaginator.
validated_findings.root_cause: Asymmetric, unvalidated 'negative offset support' added to the shared hot path of BasePaginator.get_result with a comment asserting nonexistent ORM boundary handling.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Revert to the original `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])`, or validate `cursor.offset >= 0` and raise `BadPaginationError` so callers get a 400; delete the inaccurate comment block.
validated_findings.title: BasePaginator clamps negative offsets only for forward cursors, silently masking invalid cursors and leaving prev-cursor negative offsets to crash
validated_findings.trigger: Any endpoint using BasePaginator-derived paginators receives a cursor with a negative offset (`Cursor.from_string` accepts them): forward cursors like `0:-50:0` are now silently clamped to page 0 instead of being rejected; prev cursors like `100:-3:1` still pass the negative offset into `queryset[-3:...]`.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Lines 182-184 show asymmetric handling: forward cursors clamp negative offsets via `max(0, offset)`, but prev cursors pass offset directly. Prev cursor with negative offset like `100:-3:1` passes negative to queryset slice, raising ValueError. Comment at L181 falsely claims queryset handles boundary conditions.

validated_findings.body: The comment asserts that negative offsets are a supported, efficient feature, but downstream Django queryset slicing raises on negative offsets; future maintainers may build on this false guarantee.
validated_findings.evidence:
# Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios
        # This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets
validated_findings.failure_mode: Stale/incorrect documentation misleads reviewers and future callers about cursor offset semantics.
validated_findings.impact: The comment asserts that negative offsets are a supported, efficient feature, but downstream Django queryset slicing raises on negative offsets; future maintainers may build on this false guarantee.
validated_findings.root_cause: Documentation-only change asserting behavior that neither this class nor its consumers support.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Delete the two comment lines (or replace with a note that offsets are expected to be non-negative and should be validated by consumers).
validated_findings.title: Misleading comment in Cursor.__init__ claims negative-offset support that the class does not implement
validated_findings.trigger: Any developer reading `Cursor.__init__`; no code in this class changed — `self.offset = int(offset)` behaves exactly as before.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Lines 26-27 add comment claiming negative offsets enable 'efficient reverse pagination' but no code in Cursor class changed (L28 is same `self.offset = int(offset)`). Downstream slicing raises on negative offsets, making comment misleading.
